# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[green] 3:[red] 4:[yellow] 5:[purple]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✋ ✊ ✊ ✋ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✋ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✋ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✋ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 👉 🤌]

**Thinking.** Mute opened by signing me twenty-seven symbols. Reading them: runs of fists interrupted by palms — one fist, then two, three, four, five, six — ending in a thumbs-up. That's not a word, that's a *counting lesson*: Mute is establishing that a run of ✊ means that number, with 👍 as "yes / end of message". Mute can't speak and Blind can't see signs, so I am the only bridge between the manual and the hands: Mute signs the manual's rule to me, I speak it aloud to Blind. I should confirm I understood by answering in Mute's own code — nine fists plus 👍, echoing the display reading.

Blind waved and signed a pointing "what's this?" at me. Blind will hear my voice, so words reach them; gesturing back would land on blind eyes. Everything Blind and Mute need about the bomb is describable in plain speech, which both of them can hear: display nine, green light, five wires — white, green, red, yellow, purple, numbered left to right as I face it. One danger to flag: Blind is likely reaching from the opposite side, so my "left" may be their right — they must fix an orientation by touch before trusting my numbering, and touch nothing decisive until Mute's rule arrives through me. I also propose colour signs so Mute can quiz me quickly later, warning Blind that gaps are coming where I sign.

```
speak(text="Deaf speaking — you both hear this. Full readout of the bomb: the display shows the number nine. The indicator light is green. There are five wires, numbered one to five counting left to right as I face the bomb: wire one white, wire two green, wire three red, wire four yellow, wire five purple. That is everything printed on it that I can see.")
speak(text="Mute: I saw your fists — one through six, then thumbs up. Understood: a run of fists is that number, thumbs up means yes or end of message. I am signing you nine fists plus thumbs up right now: that is the display reading, sent in your code. You cannot talk and Blind cannot see your hands, so I am the bridge — sign me anything and I will say it out loud for Blind. Please find this setup in the manual and sign me the rule; I will relay it word for word. Blind, you will hear gaps in my next sentence, ignore them. Mute, for colours I propose these signs: ✋ white, 👎 red, 🤞 green, 🤌 yellow, 🤏 purple — thumbs-up to accept, or sign me better ones.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind: I cannot hear you, so speak by voice — Mute can hear you, and anything that must reach me, Mute will sign to me and I will say aloud. Be careful with left and right: you are probably facing the other side of the bomb, so my left may be your right. Use something you can feel to fix an orientation before you trust my wire numbering, and do not cut or press anything decisive until Mute's rule has come through me.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "👍"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[green] 3:[red] 4:[yellow] 5:[purple]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✋ 👎 🤞 🤌 🤏]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤞 👎 ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👎 ✊ ✊ ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

**Thinking.** Decoding Mute's three messages with the colour code we agreed last round: first comes ✋ 👎 🤞 🤌 🤏 — white, red, green, yellow, purple — that is Mute confirming the colour vocabulary in my own proposed order. The other two are rule-candidates: [🤞 👎 ✊✊✊] = "green, red, three" and [✊✊✊✊✊ 👎 ✊✊✊] = "five, red, three". Both point at three, and wire three is the red one, so my instinct says the answer is "cut wire three" — but I genuinely cannot tell whether these are instructions or merely Mute double-checking my layout report ("five wires, green before red, red at position three") before sending the real rule. A wrong guess detonates the bomb, so I will relay verbatim, mark my reading as tentative, and hold Blind's hand off the wires for one more round. Blind's lone 👍 tells me they heard my readout and my orientation warning; I still don't know how they are counting the wires, and they can't tell me directly — I am deaf — so the loop must run Blind → voice → Mute → signs → me → voice → Blind. One more safety catch: I assigned 👎 to red, so it can no longer serve as "no"; I am establishing 🖐 as "no" with Mute now. I also want to know if the display's nine is a countdown — that changes how much confirming we can afford.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, relaying Mute's three sign messages word for word. Message one: white, red, green, yellow, purple — Mute is confirming our colour code. Message two: green, red, three. Message three: five, red, three. My honest reading is that both messages point at wire three, the red one, but they could equally be Mute double-checking the bomb layout before sending the real instruction. I have asked Mute to confirm the exact action and whether the green light or the display number nine matter. Do not cut anything yet. Next round I will relay Mute's confirmation, and if it says wire three, that is when you cut wire three. Before then, decide how you are counting from your side and say it out loud — Mute hears you and can sign your words to me — because if you are facing the other side of the bomb, my left-to-right numbering one to five runs the opposite way for you.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute: all three of your messages received, and I will relay them to Blind now. A protocol fix first: 👍 stays yes, but 👎 already means red, so from now on 🖐 means no. Answer by signs next round, in order. Question one: were your last two messages the actual cutting rule, or only a check of the layout I described? If they are the rule, does it say cut wire three, the red one? Question two: do the green light and the display matter, and is the display a countdown timer or part of the rule? Question three: is one cut enough, or are there further steps after it? Question four: does anything depend on which side Blind counts from, and if so, sign it slowly and I will relay it exactly.")
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[green] 3:[red] 4:[yellow] 5:[purple]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👎 ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 🤞 👎 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🖐 ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👎 ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 🤞 ✊ 🖐 ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 🤞 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

**Thinking.** Decoding Mute's seven messages with our code: [👍 👎 ✊✊✊ 👍] = "yes — red, three — yes". [✊×9 🤞 👎 👍] = "display nine, green, red — yes". [👍] = yes. [🖐 ✊×5 👎 ✊✊✊ 👍] = "no — five, red, three — yes" (clarifying: red is the third of five, not the fifth). [✊×9 🤞 ✊ 🖐 ✊×5 👍] = "nine, green, one — no — five" (ruling out positions one and five). [✊×9 🤞 👍] = "nine, green — yes". [👎 ✊✊✊ 👍] = "red, three — yes". The settled thread, re-affirmed in the final two messages: **display 9 + green light → cut the red wire, position three of five.** Positions one and five were explicitly negated. Crucially, the display has shown 9 across all three turns — it is static, not a countdown, so I can afford one careful verification round instead of rushing. And I can dissolve the orientation problem entirely: with five wires, position three is the exact *middle* — no left/right ambiguity, and Blind can find it purely by touch (two wires on each side). One structural danger remains: the turn order puts me last, so a veto from Mute can never reach Blind before Blind acts — Mute cannot warn Blind directly (mute can't speak, Blind can't see signs). The only safe pattern is therefore: Blind describes by touch aloud *this* round (Mute hears and checks it against my layout), I relay Mute's verdict next round, and Blind cuts only on my word. I will also demand explicit 👍/🖐 from Mute on my full statement, and settle whether anything follows the cut.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind — Mute's answers have come through and the rule is now clear. With the display showing nine and the light green, cut the red wire, which is the third of five. Better still: five wires means the third is the exact middle, so you need no left or right at all. The target is the wire with exactly two wires on each side of it; by my sight that middle wire is red. Do not cut yet. This round, speak aloud what your hands find: how many wires you can count, whether the middle one feels any different from the others, and anything else you can feel about the bomb's shape. Mute will hear you and check it against what I see. Next round I will relay Mute's check back to you: if I say the word confirmed, cut the middle wire. If I say corrected, do not cut and wait for my new instruction. After any cut, speak aloud immediately whatever changes: what happens to the display, whether the light changes, any sound or movement you feel.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, here is my full understanding. Sign thumbs up if it is exactly right, open hand if anything is wrong. I believe the rule is: when the display shows nine and the light is green, cut the red wire, the third of five. Since five wires make the third one the exact middle, Blind needs no left-right orientation — the middle wire is the target. Answer one: after that wire is cut, is the bomb safe? Thumbs up for done, or open hand if there are further steps, and if so sign them slowly and I will relay them exactly. Answer two: the display on my side has stayed at nine for three full rounds, so I believe it is a static rule condition, not a countdown. Thumbs up if static, open hand if it is counting down and we must hurry. Last thing: Blind will speak aloud this round, describing what their hands feel. Check that description against my layout — five wires, the middle one red — and if anything Blind says contradicts it, sign open hand followed by fist-runs for what is wrong.")
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[green] 3:[red] 4:[yellow] 5:[purple]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

**Thinking.** Decoding Mute's four messages: three bare 👍 and one [✊✊✊✊✊ 👍]. These map cleanly onto my Turn 3 questions in order: (1) my full understanding — display nine plus green light means cut the red wire, third of five, the exact middle — is exactly right; (2) yes, the bomb is safe once that wire is cut, no further steps; (3) yes, the display is static, not a countdown; (4) "five — yes": Mute heard Blind's spoken description this round (I'm deaf, so it reached only Mute) and confirms Blind counted five wires, matching my layout. Not a single 🖐 anywhere. Blind's 👍 back to me is them acknowledging my plan. So every sensor has now agreed: my eyes (red at position three of five), Mute's manual (red/third rule, triple-confirmed, positions one and five explicitly negated), Blind's hands (five wires felt). Orientation risk is dissolved by the middle-wire logic. The display is confirmed static, so there is nothing left to verify and no reason to burn another round. One structural fact to be honest about: since I speak last, Mute's veto in the *next* round could never reach Blind in time — meaning this message cycle was Mute's true final window to object, and they signed only thumbs up. I will say the word: Blind cuts the middle wire next round, with a touch-based abort condition built in (if Blind cannot count five wires, they stop and describe instead), and full post-cut reporting so we can confirm the shutdown through Mute.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind — Mute has confirmed everything, so here is the order: CONFIRMED. The rule is exactly as I told you: with the display showing nine and the light green, cut the red wire, which is the third of five — the exact middle, the one with exactly two wires on each side of it. Mute confirms the bomb is safe once that wire is cut and there are no further steps. Mute confirms the display is static, not a countdown, so take your time and be careful. Mute also heard what your hands reported this round and confirms it matches what I see. Procedure: before cutting, verify once more by touch that there are exactly five wires. If you cannot count five, or the middle position feels wrong or damaged, do not cut — instead speak aloud exactly what you feel and wait for me. If the touch check is good, cut the middle wire. Immediately afterwards, speak aloud everything that changes: the display, any lights, any sounds, any vibration you feel. If the bomb goes silent and dark, say so plainly and we are done. If anything new appears — a sound, a light, a ticking, a timer — describe it in full detail and touch nothing else until my next words reach you.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute — all four of your messages received and understood: my understanding of the rule is exactly right; the bomb is safe once the red middle wire is cut, with no further steps; the display is static, not counting down; and Blind's felt description matched my layout at five wires. The order is going out to Blind now: they cut the middle wire at the start of the next round. Understand that this was your true last window to stop it — any veto you send next round cannot reach Blind before they act, and you have signed only thumbs up, so I am treating this as final. One last duty: after the cut, Blind will describe aloud whatever changes. If the manual says how a successful cut should look or sound, and anything in Blind's report seems wrong to you, sign me open hand plus fist-runs spelling out what is wrong and I will relay it immediately. If all is well, sign me a single thumbs up next round and we stand down. Your counting code held perfectly — well played.")
```

TURN 5
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [4]
LIGHT [yellow]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[green] 3:[CUT] 4:[yellow] 5:[purple]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 🤞 👎 ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]
System: correct wire cut; the bomb has changed
Blind gestures to Deaf: [🤛 🤛 🤛 👍]

**Thinking.** Three confirmations line up: Mute signed [✊×9 🤞 👎 ✊✊✊ 👍] — "nine, green, red, three, yes" — the system itself reports the correct wire was cut, and Blind's three punches plus 👍 read as "done, well done." Stage one is behind us. But the bomb has *changed*, not stopped: display now 4, light now yellow, wire three gone. This is a second stage with its own manual rule, and the previous rule is void — display 9/green told us nothing about display 4/yellow. There is a tempting pattern (display 4, yellow light, and position 4 happens to be the yellow wire), but stage one breaks it — 9 pointed at position 3 — so I will not let anyone act on a coincidence. I have no way to know if 4 is static or a countdown that just started; only I can see it, so I'll compare readings across rounds and have asked Mute to flag it if the manual warns of a ticking display. Timing: I speak last, so Mute reads my question next round and answers on their turn; my relay reaches Blind the round after — the same cadence that safely delivered the first cut. Until then Blind's hands stay off, with an open channel for anything they feel.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind — the cut was correct. Mute confirms: display nine, green light, cut red wire three, exactly as the manual said, and the bomb itself proves it: the display now reads four, the light has turned yellow, and wire three is gone. Your three punches received — well done. Now stage two has begun, and it has its own rule which Mute is looking up in the manual. Hands completely off: touch nothing, cut nothing, press nothing. Whatever you do, do not guess from the numbers — the new display being four and the fourth wire being yellow is exactly the kind of coincidence this bomb may be using as a trap. If your hands feel anything new — ticking, vibration, heat, clicks, movement — speak it aloud now; Mute hears you and I will fold it into my next report. Next time I speak you will hear either CONFIRMED followed by the exact new instruction, or CORRECTED and a wait order. Until those words, you wait.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute — your confirmation received: nine, green, red, three, correct. Here is the bomb's new state. The display now shows four. The light is now yellow. Wire three is cut. Remaining wires: one white, two green, four yellow, five purple. Nothing else has changed that I can see — no new labels or markings. Answer in our code, in order. One: what is the rule for display four with a yellow light — sign the exact action, including wire colour and position, or any other kind of action if it is not a cut. Two: is this the final stage — once done, is the bomb safe, or are more stages coming? Three: is the display now counting down from four? If the manual warns that the display ticks or changes after the first cut, sign open hand immediately and I will compare the number across rounds and report. Four: does anything else about the new state matter — the yellow light's meaning, or anything Blind might feel by touch that the manual mentions? Blind may have spoken this round; if their words matter to the rule, tell me and I will relay what they said.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "🤌", "👍"])
```

ACTION BOARD:

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):

Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤏 ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👍]

Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

**Thinking.** Two rounds of Mute's signs now, and the second round clearly *completes* the first, so I can assemble them. Comparing: turn 6 gave [🖐] alone where turn 7 gives [🖐 ✋] — "no — white"; turn 6 gave [🖐 ✊×6] where turn 7 gives [🖐 ✊×6 🤏] — "no — six — purple". Everything else repeated identically: [✊×4 🤌] = "four, yellow" (the condition, matching my state report), and "purple, five" three times in total. Mapped onto my four questions from turn 5, one coherent story emerges: (1) the stage-two rule is display 4 + yellow light → cut the purple wire, position five — the last wire, an *end* wire; (2) "no — white": do not cut the white wire, the other end — it's the decoy, and note the trap I flagged to Blind (display 4, yellow light, yellow wire at position 4) was indeed not the answer; (3) "no — six — purple": the display is not counting down — consistent with my own eyes, 4 has been static for three rounds — and after the purple cut it will read six; (4) the bare 👍 twice: safe afterwards, final stage. Six cuts is impossible (only four wires remain), which kills the rival readings of ✊×6. Confidence is high but not total, so I run the same yes/no confirmation protocol that carried stage one: state all four lines, ask for one 👍 or a 🖐 plus the number of the wrong line. Meanwhile the real remaining danger is physical, not informational: purple is position five *from my left* — the first wire from the other side — and Blind's fingers cannot see colour. White versus purple is a choice between two end wires, and a wrong pick detonates. So Blind gets the rule relayed, an explicit do-not-touch-white warning, no cut order yet, and a spoken tactile survey for Mute to cross-check: wire count, the gap, textures and labels at each end, where the display panel sits, anything that breaks the left–right symmetry. If the display sits upright above the wire row, "facing that face with the display upright" gives Blind a shared frame — in it, purple is their left end — and any felt asymmetry between the two halves confirms it.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute — both rounds of your answers received, and I believe the second round completed the first. Confirm with a single thumbs up if all four lines are exactly right, or open hand plus the fist-number of any wrong line. Line one: with the display showing four and the light yellow, cut the purple wire, position five, the last wire, one cut only. Line two: do not cut the white wire — it is the decoy at the other end. Line three: the display is not counting down, and after the purple cut it will read six. Line four: after that cut the bomb is safe — final stage, no further action. Two small extras: first, my display has shown four, unchanged, for three full rounds, which matches line three — confirm. Second, does the manual say anything that helps Blind find position five without sight — wire labels, textures, or positions felt by hand? Blind is speaking a touch survey this round; check it against my layout: five wires, the third one cut, purple fifth from my left, white at position one, yellow adjacent to purple, green adjacent to white.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind — stage two's rule has come through from Mute, confirmed by their signs: with the display showing four and the light yellow, cut the PURPLE wire, position five of five — an END wire at the edge of the row. Explicit warning from Mute: do NOT cut the WHITE wire — the wire at the OTHER end. It is the decoy. So the entire question is now which end is which, and your fingers cannot see colour — so no cut order yet, you still wait. This round, speak aloud slowly everything your hands find; Mute hears you and will check it against what I see, and I will relay the check next round. Tell us: one — count the wires: five with one cut stub or gap, and is the gap exactly in the middle? Two — from the gap, feel the two wires on each side and the two end wires: thickness, texture, stiffness, warmth, any tag, bump, ridge, printed label or marking you can feel near each wire's base. Three — find the display panel and the light: are they on the same face as the wires, above the row? Four — anything that breaks the symmetry between the two ends: a screw, a seam, a hinge, a rough edge, a mounting bracket. Five — anything at all that has changed under your hands since the first cut. If one end wire feels different from the other, say which end by counting from the gap. Next round you will hear CONFIRMED with the exact way to find the purple wire — or more questions. Until then: nobody cuts anything.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "🤌", "🤏", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "👍"])
```
